findings.title: Twilight Struggle is the only shipped design whose influence loop is a solved Cold War loop — every number in it is worth stealing
findings.detail: Influence unit: 1-point tokens per country, placed only ADJACENT to a country you already control (or to your own border). Lock-in: each country has a printed Stability (1-5); you CONTROL it when your influence ≥ stability + opponent's influence. Cheap flip: the COUP — d6 + ops − 2×stability; a coup in a 'battleground' country lowers DEFCON one step (escalation coupling built in: a DEFCON-2 coup risk ends the game for the aggressor). Slow reversal: REALIGNMENT rolls with bonuses for adjacency and existing influence — this is the anti-snowball valve. Scoring: periodic regional scoring cards (Presence / Domination / Control with battleground counts, e.g. Europe 3/7/auto-win) — the exact shape of UGS's era-checkpoint victory. Failure modes: none of tedium (2-player, zero-sum), but the well-known critique is that the game has no non-aligned pole: every country is a bipolar contest, and 'the third world' only matters through scoring cards. Opportunity cost is the whole engine — ops points spent on influence are ops not spent on Space Race or events. This matches the espionage research's principle #2 (covert action as opportunity cost) and gives pillar 2 the same skeleton.
findings.evidence: Twilight Struggle (GMT Games, 2005, Ananda Gupta & Jason Matthews; digital ed. Playdek 2016) rulebook §6-7 (influence, coups, realignment), §10 (scoring); DEFCON rule 8.2; docs/research/espionage.md principle 2 already adopts the ops-point opportunity-cost model.

findings.title: Balance of Power (Crawford, 1985/1990) is the original Cold War influence game and its documented lessons are: deniable instruments are the juiciest, prestige-at-stake must be legible, and Finlandization is a passive drift toward the nearest threat
findings.detail: Per country: government affinity to each superpower, government strength, insurgency strength, plus a treaty ladder (none → diplomatic → trade → military aid → alliance-grade). Player verbs, each at magnitude 1-5: Economic Aid, Military Aid, Insurgency Aid (to rebels), Intervene for government / for insurgents, Destabilize (covert), Diplomatic Pressure, Treaty. Each action the rival may protest → crisis ladder → back down (lose prestige) or escalate (nuclear war = 'We do not reward failure'). Scoring: Prestige = Σ (relationship × the country's geopolitical weight) — i.e. weighted alignment, not count of allies. FINLANDIZATION: countries with a hostile superpower neighbor drift toward it passively — the game's only 'no-verb' alignment mover. The 1990 edition added autonomous minor-power behavior (minors act on each other) because the 1985 model made every change a superpower's doing. Crawford's own retrospectives name the legibility failure: players could not see why a given action put so much prestige at stake, which he tried to fix with closeup panels and advisory text — a direct ancestor of UGS's 'computed verdict sentence' rule.
findings.evidence: Chris Crawford, 'Balance of Power: International Politics as the Ultimate Global Game' (Microsoft Press, 1986) — full model exposition; Balance of Power: The 1990 Edition (Mindscape, 1989); Crawford, 'Chris Crawford on Game Design' (New Riders, 2003), ch. on Balance of Power.

findings.title: Victoria 2's sphere system proves that a slot-limited, passively-accruing influence budget feels right — and that unpriced reversal produces 'sphere ping-pong' and discredit spam
findings.detail: Influence unit: a per-target daily accrual for each Great Power, capped by a small number of national-focus/influence slots (the cost is attention, not treasury). Spend ladder on a target: Increase Opinion moves Hostile→Opposed→Neutral→Cordial→Friendly (~50 influence a rung); Discredit (~25), Expel Advisors (~50), Ban Embassy (~65) attack a rival's accrual; Add to Sphere (100, requires Friendly AND being the top influencer); Remove from Sphere (100). Lock-in matters mechanically: sphere = common market (trade priority), CB drag, and the leader is dragged into the sphereling's wars. Failure modes documented across the Paradox forums 2011-2014: (a) AI 'discredit/ban-embassy wars' where two GPs alternately zero each other's accrual forever; (b) ping-pong — a minor flipped in and out of spheres every few months as whoever hit 100 first clicked; (c) no organic exit — spherelings never drift, only wars or rank loss end membership; (d) the daily click cadence (bank hits 100 → click) is exactly the 'upkeep is a player job' pattern the espionage house rules ban. Fixes players shipped: HPM/HFM mods rewrote sphere rules for China substates and added 'sphere of influence' decisions with cooldowns; Heart of Darkness (Apr 2013) added rank-scaled influence targets and Great Wars so that sphere fights became war reasons rather than click races.
findings.evidence: Victoria 2 (Paradox, Aug 2010; A House Divided Feb 2012; Heart of Darkness Apr 2013) — Paradox wiki 'Influence' and 'Sphere of influence' pages for action costs and opinion rungs; Historical Project Mod / HFM changelogs; recurring forum threads titled around 'influence war' / 'AI ban embassy spam' (Paradox Interactive Forums, Victoria 2 subforum, 2011-2014).

findings.title: Victoria 3's Sphere of Influence DLC (1.7, June 2024) is the latest attempt at exactly UGS's problem — leverage over a country accrues from structural ties, and foreign LOBBIES inside interest groups are how the per-faction model was shipped; the community's verdict was 'too passive, too spreadsheet'
findings.detail: Power Blocs: a leader accumulates LEVERAGE over each country from trade volume, migration, diplomatic pacts, subjecthood and proximity; when the leader's leverage beats the target's own it may 'sway' and invite; bloc COHESION is the lock-in — low cohesion and members leave. Per-faction: interest groups form pro-/anti-country lobbies weighted by leverage; lobbies push relations and the acceptance of invitations — the first shipped Paradox model where a foreign power acts on a domestic faction rather than on the country scalar. Diplomatic Plays (base 1.0) are an escalation ladder (maneuvers → warning phase → back-down or war) that UGS's escalation pillar already parallels. What players said (1.7-1.8 feedback threads): leverage is 'wait and watch' with no verb to accelerate it; blocs read as a bonus spreadsheet; AI joins and leaves for opaque reasons; the lobby system is invisible until it fires. Paradox's 1.8 'Masala Chai' patch retuned leverage and added lobby interaction — the fix was more verbs pointed at the lobbies, confirming the direction: factions as the target of verbs, structural ties as the passive floor.
findings.evidence: Victoria 3 (Paradox, Oct 2022); Sphere of Influence DLC + patch 1.7 'Kahwah' (24 June 2024); Vic3 dev diaries on Power Blocs, Leverage and Lobbies (spring 2024, dev diary series ~#108-#116); 1.8 'Masala Chai' patch notes (Nov 2024); Paradox forum 1.7 feedback threads on leverage/blocs.

findings.title: HoI4 shows the anti-patterns: a hoardable single currency (Political Power), a 'Boost Party Popularity' slider that makes ideology drift a bank withdrawal, a 'Stage Coup' button, and a Non-Aligned ideology that is literally a void
findings.detail: Unit: Political Power, ~2/day, hoarded and spent on everything (advisors, decisions, diplomacy). Ideology per country = four party popularities; base-game diplomatic action 'Boost Party Popularity' (PP-denominated, continuous) raises a target's party share; 'Stage Coup' fires once popularity clears a floor and ships equipment to a rebel side → civil war. La Résistance (25 Feb 2020) moved both to named operatives ('Boost ideology' mission, 'Stage coup' operation) — which made them slower but added the maintenance loop the espionage research condemned. Together for Victory (Dec 2016) added the one good idea: AUTONOMY as a bidirectional commitment score (Integrated Puppet → Puppet → Colony → Dominion → Free), raised by the subject's contribution and lowered by the overlord's lend-lease — subjects earn their way out, overlords buy them back in. Failure modes on record: PP hoarding turns influence into a late-game shopping spree; 'ideology drift defense' national spirits had to be added because AI minors flipped absurdly; coup cheese (flip a neighbor with a few thousand rifles); 'Neutrality' has no faction, no goals and no pull, so a non-aligned world is a dead world. Mods that reworked the space (Cold War: Iron Curtain, Millennium Dawn, TNO) all replaced popularity with scripted per-country political trees or a numeric 'influence' with decisions on cooldown — i.e. they added lock-in and cadence.
findings.evidence: Hearts of Iron IV (Paradox, June 2016); Together for Victory (15 Dec 2016) autonomy system; La Résistance (25 Feb 2020) operatives/operations; HoI4 wiki 'Diplomacy' (Boost Party Popularity, Stage Coup) and 'Subject' pages; Cold War: Iron Curtain – A World Divided and Millennium Dawn mod design notes; docs/research/espionage.md §1 on the La Résistance tedium thread.

findings.title: Terra Invicta's control points + public opinion is the closest modern model of 'alignment per faction inside a country' and it produced the genre's most cited whack-a-mole
findings.detail: Each nation has N control points (scaled by size); factions take CPs with councilor missions ('Control Nation'), remove others' with 'Purge', and move the substrate — per-nation PUBLIC OPINION toward each faction — with 'Public Campaign'. Opinion is the lock-in: a CP held against hostile opinion is cheap to purge, one held with majority support is expensive and generates unrest when purged. Capital CP is privileged (holds executive verbs: national policy, priorities). Coups are a councilor mission against military CPs. What went wrong (Steam/Discord 2022-2024): 'councilor micro is not fun'; factions purge each other's CPs every turn in Nigeria/Kazakhstan-tier nations with nobody committing; Pavonis's successive Early Access patches added scaling CP upkeep (influence per CP, superlinear), purge cost escalation and unrest from repeated purges — i.e. they had to add hysteresis and price reversals after launch. Take-away for UGS: opinion-as-substrate is right, per-CP tokens and per-turn missions are the wrong cadence; the fix that worked was making reversal cost grow with recency and having a commitment lock (opinion majority) that verbs cannot bypass.
findings.evidence: Terra Invicta (Pavonis Interactive / Hooded Horse, Early Access 26 Sept 2022 onward) — in-game Codex 'Control Points', 'Public Opinion', 'Purge'; Pavonis EA patch notes on control-point maintenance and purge costs (0.3.x line, 2022-2023); Steam discussions 'councilor micro' / 'CP whack-a-mole'; also cited in docs/research/espionage.md §9.

findings.title: The small-state political games (Hidden Agenda 1988, Suzerain 2020, Kremlingames, Rogue State) all converge on the same interior model: 3-5 named domestic factions each with a foreign patron, and aid that comes with strings
findings.detail: Hidden Agenda (1988): you run 'Chimerica' after a revolution; three factions (left/centre/right) fill cabinet posts; the US embassy and Cuba/USSR each offer aid tied to policy; the ending is 'The Verdict of History', a retrospective score — alignment as the sum of who holds which ministries. Suzerain (2020): Sordland between the US-analog ATO/CSP and the Soviet-analog Bludish Union; your budget is tiny, so alignment is bought with treaty signatures, base rights and constitutional choices, and every domestic faction (Old Guard, Reform, oligarchs, military, unions) has a leader with a legible stance; commitment is a signed treaty act you cannot unsign without a crisis. Kremlingames (Crisis in the Kremlin 2017, Ostalgie 2018, China: Mao's Legacy 2019): Politburo factions with support levels; satellites have loyalty that decays unless subsidized; in Ostalgie the exogenous variable is Moscow's own drift (Gorbachev) — satellites face a patron they cannot control. Rogue State (2015/Revolution 2021): four factions with approval, US/Russia/China relations, neighbor pressure, coups against YOU. Common shape: alignment = which coalition governs; foreign powers spend on factions; aid has policy strings; the drift (satellite loyalty) is an upkeep that costs the patron. Also convergent: none of them let a foreign power 'set alignment' directly — the government changes, the alignment follows.
findings.evidence: Hidden Agenda (Springboard Software / Jim Gasperini, 1988); Suzerain (Torpor Games, 4 Dec 2020); Crisis in the Kremlin (Kremlingames, 2017 remake of the 1991 Spectrum HoloByte original), Ostalgie: The Berlin Wall (2018), China: Mao's Legacy (2019); Rogue State (LRDG, 2015), Rogue State Revolution (Modern Wolf, Mar 2021).

findings.title: Subject-drift mechanics that worked (Stellaris Overlord loyalty, EU4 liberty desire) price the patron's bloc in ongoing politics, not money — and give the rival a clean counter-verb
findings.detail: EU4: each subject has Liberty Desire (0-100%) fed by its development relative to the overlord, the overlord's actions, and rival 'Support Independence'; above 50% the subject may join an independence war. Rights of Man (Oct 2016) added Trust/Favors as spendable lock-in with allies. Stellaris Overlord (12 May 2022): subject Loyalty (−100..+100) moves monthly by the fairness of negotiated agreement terms (taxes, basic/specialist type, holdings) — harsh terms hold the subject economically but bleed loyalty; loyalty below zero flips to an independence faction. Both are the same lesson as the UGS sketch's 'mirror': keeping a satellite is a standing political price paid in terms the satellite's own factions read, and the rival's verb is to raise that price (Support Independence). Failure modes: EU4 diplomat babysitting ('improve relations' on 8 subjects forever — a mandatory upkeep loop later softened by auto-actions and 'Diplomatic Feedback'), and Stellaris's contract renegotiation micro. Rule extracted: drift must be readable from a single line ('EAST GERMANY: LOYALTY SLIPPING — TERMS RESENTED, WESTERN BROADCASTS REACH 60%'), and the counter-verb (crackdown) must cost world opinion, not merely money.
findings.evidence: Europa Universalis IV (Paradox, 2013) wiki 'Liberty desire', 'Subject nation'; Rights of Man (11 Oct 2016) Trust/Favors; Stellaris: Overlord (12 May 2022) dev diaries #246-#250 on subject loyalty and agreement terms; Stellaris Federations (17 Mar 2020) for envoys as a slot budget (3-5 envoys assigned to improve/harm relations); Nemesis (15 Apr 2021) envoys→spy networks.

findings.title: Every system that let a superpower purchase alignment with a fungible bank snowballed; every system that priced influence in attention slots and escalation headroom stayed contested
findings.detail: Bank-denominated systems (HoI4 PP, Superpower 2 treasury-funded treaties, Supreme Ruler: Cold War's relations spend) let the richer side buy the map late-game and are the source of 'ahistorical blob' complaints. Slot-denominated systems (Vic2 focus slots, EU4 diplomats, Stellaris envoys, TS ops points) cap concurrent commitments so the choice is WHERE, not how much; they stayed interesting for the whole run. The second stabilizer is coupling to escalation: TS's DEFCON-degrading coups and BoP's crisis ladder both make the fast verbs spend a shared global resource — UGS's Tension is that resource and it already exists. The third stabilizer is regional periodic scoring that rewards presence in many contested regions over deep control of a few (TS's scoring cards; BoP's weighted prestige), which counters rich-get-richer because marginal influence in a region you dominate scores nothing. Superpower 2 (2004) and Realpolitiks (2017) are the negative controls: influence as an undifferentiated 'relations' number spent from budget, with no lock-in ladder and no escalation price — reviewed as 'a spreadsheet where everyone hates you'.
findings.evidence: Superpower 2 (GolemLabs/DreamCatcher, 2004) contemporary reviews (GameSpot, IGN 2004); Supreme Ruler: Cold War (BattleGoat, 2011); Realpolitiks (Jujubee, 2017); Terminal Conflict (Strategy Mill, 2019) as a real-time TS descendant with an ops-point budget and DEFCON; Twilight Struggle rulebook §8.2; Crawford 1986 prestige formula.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Alignment as a per-country signed score with a hysteresis commitment ladder that DERIVES the existing three-valued enum
mechanics_recommendations.why: Every working system had a ladder with asymmetric costs (Vic2 opinion rungs → sphere; TS control threshold = stability; HoI4 autonomy tiers). Vic2's ping-pong and Terra Invicta's whack-a-mole both came from thresholds you cross both ways at the same price. The war slice already stores a finer scale (occupation-zone `alignment: i16, −1000..1000`), and `Military::alignment_of` is the single read-point, so a finer score can feed the enum without touching 30 downstream reads.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Per country: `lean: i16` (−1000 East .. +1000 West) plus `commitment: Contested | Leaning | Aligned | Treaty | Satellite` with a band per commitment. Entering a higher band needs lean past the entry threshold for N consecutive months; falling out needs lean below a LOWER exit threshold (hysteresis ~±150). `alignment_of` returns EasternBloc/WesternBloc only at Aligned or above; Leaning still reads NonAligned for basing/red-lines (so a leaning state is not yet a target set). Treaty/Satellite are only set by an explicit act (treaty event, client-state creation from war-termination, scripted SetAlignment) and cost a Tension delta to break. Read by the player as one line in the dossier: 'IRAN — LEANING WEST (+220), NOT ALIGNED: GOVERNMENT FRIENDLY, ARMY FRIENDLY, STREET HOSTILE'.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Three named factions per country — Government, Army, Street — each with its own disposition; alignment lean is the Government's disposition; elections and coups swap which faction governs
mechanics_recommendations.why: This is the convergent interior model of Hidden Agenda, Suzerain, Kremlingames, Rogue State and Vic3's lobbies, sized to the espionage rule of ~5 tracked threads: three is enough for covert ops to target one faction (arm the army, fund the party, broadcast to the street) without a Vic3-style IG matrix. It answers the sketch's granularity question: per-faction, but a fixed triad, never a per-country list.
mechanics_recommendations.how: `factions: [Disposition; 3]` per country (signed permille each). Verbs move ONE faction: Aid → Government; Arms → Army; Propaganda/radio → Street; party funding (espionage op) → Street; coup sponsorship → installs Army disposition as Government, priced by stability à la TS (odds ladder from `stability_of`, exposure clock, PROVEN attribution = world-opinion hit). Elections: a per-country election calendar (data-driven, historian-sourced for the ~40 electoral states) where Government disposition is pulled toward Street each cycle in democracies; in closed states Government is only moved by aid/patron pressure or coups. Lean = Government disposition, so no verb sets alignment directly — a country changes sides because its government did, which is what the newspaper prints.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Influence programs as a capped portfolio of standing commitments (3 slots for a superpower, 1-2 for middle powers), never a spendable bank
mechanics_recommendations.why: Slot economies (Vic2 foci, EU4 diplomats, Stellaris envoys, TS ops) stayed contested for a whole campaign; bank economies (HoI4 PP) snowballed. It also satisfies the economy house rule that decision count is a designed budget (~2-4 per game-month) and the espionage rule that upkeep is never a player job.
mechanics_recommendations.how: A program = (target country, kind ∈ Aid / Military Mission / Broadcast / Diplomatic Mission, level 1-3). It is a standing monthly flow: Aid draws from the existing construction/stock pool and moves Government by a rate scaled by the target's size (small states move faster — the decolonization frontier is cheap by design); Military Mission moves Army and lowers coup odds against the patron; Broadcast moves Street and is jammed by closed regimes (rate × openness); Diplomatic Mission unlocks treaty offers once Aligned. Programs persist until reassigned; the only monthly touch is a wire line when a program's target crosses a band. Rival AI uses the same portfolio with an auto-allocator (highest contested weight × closeness to a band edge), zero bespoke logic, mirroring the economy's auto-invest default.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Non-Aligned as an active third pole born at Bandung (April 1955), with its own leverage sources and a prestige score for its leaders
mechanics_recommendations.why: HoI4's neutrality is a void; TS has no third pole; the sketch's open question is answered by history: Nehru, Tito, Nasser and Sukarno actively recruited, and Suez/Bandung moved alignment against BOTH blocs. An active pole also fixes bipolar snowballing — every bloc push into a NAM member raises the price for both sides.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Before 1955 NonAligned is the passive middle (band around lean 0). The Bandung event creates the `NonAlignedPole` with leverage sources = the aggregate weight of Contested/Leaning states whose lean is within ±150 plus named leaders (IND, YUG, EGY, IDN). Effects: NAM membership adds a per-month pull of Government toward 0 in members and multiplies both blocs' program costs in them; overt bloc coups/crackdowns anywhere (PROVEN or acknowledged) shift every NAM member's Street away from the actor — the 'world opinion' channel. NAM leaders score prestige at checkpoints by member count; a playable India/Yugoslavia gets its own program slots. Read by the player in the standings page as a third column.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Stability as the price of a flip, and the fast verbs (coup, election interference, crackdown) spend Tension and world opinion, not money
mechanics_recommendations.why: TS's coup formula (ops − 2×stability, battleground coups degrade DEFCON) and BoP's crisis ladder are why those games never let the rich side buy the map. The espionage research already holds that covert action is cheap in cash and expensive in politics, and Tension already exists as the shared escalation resource.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Coup sponsorship = an espionage op whose outcome ladder is computed from `stability_of(target)` and the Army faction's disposition (Army friendly + stability < 40 → PROBABLE; stability > 70 → UNLIKELY regardless of network). Success sets Government = Army disposition, drops stability by a data-tuned amount, and adds Tension scaled by the target's region weight (a Guatemala costs little; an Italy costs a crisis). Election interference is a cheaper op with a Street delta and a loud-failure branch that swings Street the other way (the 'backfires when blown' clause). Crackdown (the mirror verb, Hungary 1956) is a SimCommand on an own-bloc Satellite whose Street has turned: restores Government and stability, costs world opinion (Street delta in every Contested state toward the rival, NAM pull) and a Tension delta. All three are pull decisions: they appear as offers on the wire when preconditions hold, never as always-on buttons.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Decolonization as a founding window: Independence seeds the newborn's triad from the parent, the anti-colonial movement's patron and the settlement, then opens 24 months of cheap verbs before the first election or coup sets the commitment
mechanics_recommendations.why: Today a newborn's alignment is whatever the event file says. TS's adjacency rule and BoP's Finlandization both say new states should start pulled toward whoever is already present nearby; the 1960 African wave is 17 openings in one year, which is only a contest if the price of presence is low and time-boxed.
mechanics_recommendations.how: On `Independence`: Government disposition = parent bloc's lean × a colonial-legacy factor (data field on the newborn's CountryDef, sourced), Army = the parent's military-mission legacy, Street = the anti-colonial movement's patron (data field, e.g. Guinea's Street leans East, Ivory Coast's West), all scaled toward 0. A `founding_window_until` tick makes program rates ×2 and bands soft (no hysteresis) for 24 months; the first scheduled election or the first coup closes the window and fixes commitment. The newspaper's reserved 'THE COLONIAL QUESTION' section prints the open windows with their remaining months and current lean, which is the pull-style decision surface: the player sees 'CONGO: FOUNDING WINDOW 18 MONTHS, LEANING EAST (−90)' and chooses whether to spend a slot.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: INFLUENCE STANDINGS newspaper page as the scoring surface: per-region Presence / Domination / Control with battleground weights, monthly and date-stamped, printed as believed
mechanics_recommendations.why: TS's scoring cards and BoP's weighted prestige are the two scoring designs players understood; the victory doc wants era checkpoints measuring bloc alignment first; the newspaper registry reserved the section; the economy house rule wants monthly still displays and epistemic texture.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Regions (Europe, Middle East, Asia, Africa, Americas) each carry a weight table and a list of battleground tags (historian-sourced). Standing per bloc = Presence (≥1 Aligned), Domination (more Aligned + more battlegrounds than the rival), Control (all battlegrounds). The page prints one row per region with the verdict word and the two or three states closest to a band edge ('NEAREST TO MOVE: IRAN (+220 ↑), GUATEMALA (+310 ↓)'), each row deep-linking to that country's dossier and its verb buttons. Displayed lean goes through political-domain intel fidelity, so a rival satellite's true drift is a rumor until penetrated. Checkpoint years (1955, 1960...) freeze the table into the score.

pitfalls: Sphere ping-pong / whack-a-mole: symmetric flip thresholds and unpriced reversals produced Vic2's monthly sphere swaps and Terra Invicta's purge loops; UGS needs hysteresis bands, treaty rungs that cost Tension to break, and reversal cost that rises with recency.

A fungible influence bank (HoI4 political power, Superpower 2 treasury): the richer bloc buys the map by 1962 and the game snowballs; price influence in slots, Tension and world opinion, let cash be nearly trivial.

Upkeep as a player job: Vic2's 'bank hit 100, click', EU4's diplomat babysitting, HoI4 La Résistance's operative loops; standing programs must run without monthly touches and the only interrupts must be band changes and offers.

A 'Set Alignment' verb: nothing shipped that let a foreign power set a country's alignment directly stayed believable; alignment must follow a government change (election, coup, treaty) so the newspaper can report a cause.
Non-Aligned as a void (HoI4 neutrality): with no third attractor the decolonization wave collapses to a bipolar tug and the 1955-65 world reads wrong; NAM must pull and must score.
Faction bloat: Vic3's interest-group matrix and Terra Invicta's per-CP tokens are legible only with a wiki; cap at a fixed triad per country and make every faction line a verb target.

Decision count scaling with entity count: 226 countries × 3 factions × 5 verbs is a dashboard, not a game; the standings page must triage to the ~5 states nearest a band edge, and program slots must be fixed per rank.

Silent drift: alignment moving without a wire line is the espionage rule's 'silent modifier change' and reads as a bug; every band crossing, coup offer and satellite loyalty slip is a teletype item with a cause.

Superpower self-flip: SetAlignment on USA/USSR is already flagged as content-forbidden; the score system must clamp Government disposition for the two poles and treat their own Street as the domestic-opinion mirror, not as an alignment input.

Writing bespoke rival AI: the economy slice shipped with zero new AI by giving AI countries the passive default; the influence slice must do the same with an auto-allocator over the same program portfolio.
analysts.first_hour_test: Playing the USA from 1950-01-01 to the July 1950 newspaper: (1) In the first minute the standings page shows Europe DOMINATED WEST with Italy and France flagged as battlegrounds whose Street is Leaning East (the PCI/PCF vote shares), Asia CONTESTED with Iran, Indochina, Indonesia and Burma as the states nearest a band edge, and China ALIGNED EAST under the Feb-14-1950 Sino-Soviet treaty. (2) The player has three empty program slots and fills two in the first five minutes with real trade-offs: Aid to Italy (moves Government, slow) versus a Broadcast program to Eastern Europe (moves Street in Satellites, cheap, jammed) versus a Military Mission to Iran (moves Army, lowers coup odds against the Shah later). (3) Between February and May at least one wire line reports a rival program ('SOVIET AID MISSION ARRIVES IN PEKING'; 'RADIO MOSCOW EXPANDS PERSIAN SERVICE') that the player could not have caused, and one line reports the player's own program crossing a threshold. (4) By the June 1950 paper one contested country has moved a band attributable in the paper's own sentence to a player verb ('ITALY LEANING WEST — MARSHALL AID CREDITED') and the North Korean invasion event (June 25) applies the world-opinion swing to Asia's Street values so that the July standings differ from June for reasons the player can read. (5) Nothing required a click that was not a decision: no monthly upkeep, no program renewal, no more than four influence decisions in six game-months. Mirror check when playing the USSR: East Germany's Street shows Leaning West with a cause line (Western broadcasts), and a 'crackdown' offer must NOT appear yet because stability is above the threshold — the player sees the price before the 1953 uprising arrives.

findings.title: Twilight Struggle's entire contest is three integers per country: two influence piles and a stability number; control is a margin test, not a state
findings.detail: In Twilight Struggle (GMT 2005; Deluxe Ed. 2009, rules v3; Playdek digital 2016) every country carries US influence, USSR influence and a printed Stability Number 1-5. A superpower CONTROLS a country iff its influence >= opponent influence + stability. Nothing else is stored; 'the map is painted' is a derived view. Placement costs 1 OP per point unless the opponent controls the country, then 2 OP per point, and you may only place where you already have influence or adjacent to it / your own superpower. Two tuning lessons fall out: (a) denial is cheaper than acquisition (one 2-OP point breaks control; taking control needs a margin of `stability`), so the arithmetic itself produces a large contested/non-aligned middle without any third player; (b) stability is the whole difficulty surface. The UGS data cannot support this yet: 73 of 86 sovereigns sit at the flat `stability: 60`, so a coup or aid frontier derived from it would be uniform. TS's printed numbers are a sourced starting table (UK 5, W.Germany 4, Japan 4, Israel 4, France 3, Poland 3, India 3, Cuba 3, Iran 2, Egypt 2, Italy 2, Turkey 2, Pakistan 2, Guatemala 1, Zaire 1, Nigeria 1, Angola 1) and the existing 0-100 field maps cleanly with `stab_ts = clamp(round(stability/20), 1, 5)`; the 182 `AdjustStability` event effects already in the corpus then move countries across the coup frontier dynamically for free.
findings.evidence: TS Deluxe rulebook §4 (Influence), §6.1 (Control), §6.3 (Realignment), §6.4 (Coups); country stabilities from the board; twilightstrategy.com card/country analyses; repo: crates/ugs-data/src/lib.rs CountryDef.stability, assets/data/scenario/1950/countries/generated.ron stability histogram (73x60), events/*.ron AdjustStability count 182.

findings.title: The coup formula `d6 + ops - 2*stability` defines a hard frontier at stability 3; the tuning target is the frontier, not the die
findings.detail: TS coup: roll d6, add the card's ops value, subtract 2 x stability; if positive, remove that many opponent influence and place any remainder as your own. Expected value at ops 3: stab 1 = +4.5 (always lands, usually flips), stab 2 = +2.5, stab 3 = +0.5 (a coin flip that rarely flips control), stab 4 = -1.5 (only a 6 yields +1). So coups are a Third-World instrument by arithmetic, exactly the historical pattern (Syria x3 1949, Iran 1953, Guatemala 1954, Iraq 1958, Congo 1960) and never a European one. Coups in battleground countries lower DEFCON by one; coups also count toward the per-turn Military Ops requirement (you must spend >= current DEFCON in military ops or lose VP), so a cooling world *penalizes* passivity, the hawk-pressure paradox. For UGS the translation is direct because espionage already exists: `ops` = the funded network tier 0-3 in `intel.rs`, the coup is a `LaunchOperation` variant resolved from the `b"op-resolve"` stream with the outcome ladder (clean flip / flip-with-evidence / failed quietly / failed loudly / blown and PROVEN), and the visible pre-commit number is the FRONTIER, not a percentage: 'STAB 2 - NETWORK L2 - COUP: PROBABLE'. Stability is what makes Iran and Italy different targets; the die is texture.
findings.evidence: TS rules §6.4 (coup formula, battleground DEFCON drop, Military Ops), §8 (DEFCON); twilightstrategy.com 'Coups' strategy page; repo: docs/design/systems/espionage.md (network funding 0-3, op lifecycle, outcome ladder), docs/research/espionage.md principle 5 (ladders, never percentages) and 12 (covert action cheap in money, expensive in politics).

findings.title: Realignment is the adjacency mechanic: it turns regional dominance into a contiguity engine and is the reason TS maps look 'painted'
findings.detail: TS realignment: both players roll d6; each adds +1 per adjacent country they control, +1 if they have more influence in the target, +1 if the target is adjacent to their own superpower; the loser removes influence equal to the difference. A target surrounded by three of your controlled countries plus your lead is +5 vs their ~0, near-certain to strip. This is why blocs end up geographically contiguous: once you dominate a region, cleaning out the rival's remnants is cheap, and isolated outposts (Cuba, Finland) are prizes precisely because they are surrounded. Community consensus (twilightstrategy.com; BGG strategy threads) is that realignment is 'situational' and coups dominate, which is a warning: adjacency must be strong enough to matter or the verb is dead weight. UGS has province adjacency but no country adjacency graph and no notion of superpower reach; both are derivable once from `ProvinceDef.adjacent` plus a coastal flag (US naval reach to any coast; USSR land reach only until a 1960s navy event), which gives the geographic asymmetry of the real Cold War as a placement rule rather than a modifier.
findings.evidence: TS rules §6.3; twilightstrategy.com 'Realignments' page; Pax Pamir 2nd ed. (Wehrle 2019) dominance checks (a coalition leading by >=4 blocks scores; loyalty switching = bandwagoning); repo: crates/ugs-data/src/lib.rs ProvinceDef.adjacent; docs/design/systems/escalation.md (basing rights as influence content).

findings.title: Region scoring with battlegrounds is the minimum scoreboard that makes 226 countries a contest instead of a list, and it doubles as the AI's utility function
findings.detail: TS scores six regions with three tiers: Presence (control >= 1 country), Domination (more battlegrounds AND more total countries than the opponent, at least one non-battleground), Control (more total countries AND all battlegrounds). Points: Europe 3/7/auto-win, Asia 3/7/9, Middle East 3/5/7, Central America 1/3/5, South America 2/5/6, Africa 1/4/6, plus +1 per controlled battleground and +1 per controlled country adjacent to the enemy superpower. The tier structure makes a small set of named countries (~30 battlegrounds) the real board and everything else a tiebreaker, which is exactly the decision-budget principle the economic-agency research already imposes: regions are where you look, a capped set is where you act. The scoring table is also a gradient any AI can climb with a priority list; the COIN series (Fire in the Lake, GMT 2014; A Distant Plain, 2013) ships bot flowcharts that are nothing but ranked predicates over the same scoring variables, evaluated once per activation, which is the exact shape of a monthly `TickSet::Politics` system iterating sorted tags. UGS vision already names 1955/1960 checkpoints scoring bloc alignment; nothing is implemented because nothing moves alignment. Region scoring is the missing object, and its 'IF SCORED TODAY' preview is the influence-standings page the newspaper registry already reserves.
findings.evidence: TS rules §10 (Scoring) and the scoring cards; COIN series bot flowcharts (FitL playbook, ADP 2nd ed. non-player rules); repo: docs/design/vision.md Victory, docs/design/systems/newspaper.md section registry ('influence standings'), docs/research/economic-agency.md principle 3.

findings.title: DEFCON coupling is region-gating plus a battleground price, and its known exploit ('DEFCON suicide') shows what a sim must guard against
findings.detail: TS DEFCON runs 5 to 1 and improves by one each turn; a coup in a battleground drops it by one; at DEFCON 4 no coups/realignments in Europe, at 3 none in Asia either, at 2 none in the Middle East either; at 1 the phasing player loses. Regions close in the order a world war would start. The community's famous exploit, DEFCON suicide, forces the opponent to play an event that compels a battleground coup at DEFCON 2, ending the game; players learned to track who is 'forced' and when. Translating to UGS's 0-100 tension (bands Calm/Wary/Crisis/Brink at 25/50/75, start 30.0, decay ~2/day plus value/250): map the four bands to the DEFCON gates (Wary: all open; Crisis: Europe closed; Brink: Europe/Asia/Middle East closed, only Africa and Latin America open, the 1980s pattern), price a battleground coup at roughly +15.0 tension and a non-battleground at +5.0 so three battleground coups in a quarter push Wary into Crisis but decay recovers a season later (the TS per-turn +1 analog), and make a PROVEN-attributed coup against a rival-controlled battleground bank a crisis pretext through the existing attribution machine. The guard: no event option and no AI priority may ever force a coup at Brink, and the AI's risk multiplier note in tension.md already says Brink actors seek off-ramps.
findings.evidence: TS rules §8 (DEFCON) and §6.4; twilightstrategy.com 'DEFCON suicide' discussion; repo: docs/design/systems/tension.md (bands, decay, AI note), crates/ugs-sim/src/tension.rs band boundaries 250/500/750, docs/design/systems/espionage.md attribution UNATTRIBUTED/SUSPECTED/PROVEN.

findings.title: Non-Aligned in the board games is an emergent equilibrium plus a saturation rule, not a third player; the one game that made it a faction gave it its own win condition
findings.detail: TS has no NAM: the uncontrolled middle emerges because breaking control costs one 2-OP point while taking it costs a `stability` margin. Cold War: CIA vs KGB (Fantasy Flight 2007) adds the missing half: each objective (country) has a stability value that acts as a CAP; you draw influence cards blackjack-style and BUST if you exceed it, losing the country, which is Iran 1979 and Afghanistan 1979 as arithmetic: overcommitment provokes nationalist backlash. Quartermaster General: Cold War (Griggling/PSC 2019) is the only design that makes Non-Aligned a playable third faction, and it has to give it a distinct scoring rule (score on unaligned area) to work at all, which is a large AI investment. 13 Days (Jolly Roger 2016) instead treats World Opinion as one of three scored battlegrounds with its own DEFCON track, and Labyrinth (GMT 2010) modifies every 'War of Ideas' roll by a global prestige track. So the mechanism answer to the sketch's first open question: Non-Aligned is (1) the passive middle produced by denial-cheaper-than-acquisition, plus (2) an active FIELD, not an actor: a saturation backlash when either bloc's influence exceeds a stability-scaled cap, and after the Bandung event (Apr 1955) a regional decay on foreign influence emanating from NAM champions (India, Egypt, Yugoslavia, Indonesia), plus (3) a scored outcome ('denied to both') at checkpoints. That gives Nehru/Nasser/Tito teeth with zero new AI.
findings.evidence: TS rules §4.2 (2-OP placement into opponent-controlled); Cold War: CIA vs KGB rules (stability as a bust threshold); Quartermaster General: Cold War rulebook (three factions, NAM scoring); 13 Days rules (three battlegrounds incl. World Opinion); Labyrinth v3 rules (prestige modifies War of Ideas); Bandung Conference 18-24 Apr 1955, Belgrade Conference Sep 1961.

findings.title: COIN and Terra Invicta show the two-variable split that answers 'per-country or per-faction': government CONTROL vs popular SUPPORT in the same space, with factions deferred to flags
findings.detail: Fire in the Lake gives every space two independent variables: Control (COIN control if COIN pieces exceed insurgents; NVA control if NVA exceed all others) and Support/Opposition on a five-step scale (Active Support .. Active Opposition). Factions score on different ones (US on Total Support, VC on Total Opposition, NVA on Control), so allies inside a bloc have divergent goals (A Distant Plain: Coalition scores support and troops home, Government scores patronage and control: the domestic-mirror precedent). Terra Invicta (Pavonis 2022) is the real-time digital analog: nations have N control points split among factions, public opinion per faction, and unrest rises when you hold control points against opinion; its known failure is councilor micromanagement, not the model. 1989: Dawn of Freedom (GMT 2012) is the per-faction extreme: each of six countries is six societal spaces (Elite, Bureaucrats, Workers, Students, Intellectuals, Church/Farmers) contested TS-style with Power Struggles at scoring; it proves faction targeting is fun but 36 spaces is a board's limit, and 6 x 123 in a sim would violate the decision budget. Recommendation: v1 per-country influence piles (government lean); v1.5 a single popular-sympathy number per country (occupation zones in war-termination already carry a popular alignment to fold in), which sets election outcomes in democracies, insurgency/backlash risk when government and people diverge, and occupation cost; factions only as targeting flags on ops (ARMY, CHURCH, UNIONS, PARTY) following 1989, never as six more contested numbers.
findings.evidence: Fire in the Lake rules §1.6-1.7, §7 (victory); A Distant Plain 2nd ed. rules (Coalition vs Government victory); Terra Invicta control points/public opinion (Pavonis Interactive, 2022 EA); 1989: Dawn of Freedom rules §5 (spaces by social group), §11 (Power Struggles); repo: docs/design/systems/war-termination.md occupation zone 'military control vs popular alignment', docs/research/espionage.md principle 9 (no roster; Terra Invicta micro).

findings.title: Turn-to-real-time translation: the scarce quantity is total ops over the campaign, not ops per action; TS gives each side ~170 ops for 84 countries
findings.detail: TS is 10 turns over 1945-1989 with 6-8 action rounds each; a hand averages ~2.5 ops per card, so each side spends roughly 17 ops per turn and ~170 over the game, against a board whose total control cost (sum of stabilities) is several hundred. Scarcity relative to the board is the design: you cannot paint everything, so priorities are the game. The naive real-time port (an ops budget per month) overshoots by an order of magnitude: 4 ops/month is 12x TS density and paints 123 countries in eight years. Tuning anchor: campaign-total ops per superpower should stay well below the sum of control thresholds after decay and removal are counted; ~1.5-2 ops/month for a superpower in 1950 (18-24/yr), ~0.5 for UK/France/PRC, scaled by economy so pillar 4 funds pillar 2 (Marshall Plan $13.3B 1948-52; Mutual Security Act 1951; Soviet Egypt arms deal via Czechoslovakia Sep 1955; Aswan Oct 1958 as the priced auction the economic-agency doc already defers). Cadence: budgets accrue on `new_month`, player intent is queued as commands during the month, AI blocs resolve their monthly picks in sorted tag order in `TickSet::Politics` after events, and the rival's landed moves arrive as wire notices with a 'RESPOND?' pull decision, replacing TS's alternating action rounds with intent-then-event as the espionage research prescribes.
findings.evidence: TS rules §3 (turn structure, action rounds), card ops distribution; twilightstrategy.com 'Theory' pages on ops scarcity; repo: CLAUDE.md determinism (new_month cadence, sorted iteration), docs/research/espionage.md principle 3 (intent-then-event), docs/research/economic-agency.md 'Deferred: the Aswan auction'.

findings.title: 'Events the opponent must play' and the Space Race translate to the world timeline and prestige projects, which already exist; the change is converting SetAlignment decrees into influence pushes
findings.detail: TS's dilemma engine is that playing an opponent's card for ops still fires their event; the Space Race is where you dump a card you dare not let resolve. UGS already has the equivalent: 189 scripted events with `OptionChosen` chains that fire against a bloc on schedule, and `ProjectPayload::Prestige { tension_relief }` for prestige competition. What breaks the contest is that 29 events write `SetAlignment` as a decree: Cuba 1959 becomes Eastern regardless of what either bloc did there, and independence.ron gives Dahomey a fixed WesternBloc at birth. Board-game translation: scripted events should deliver INFLUENCE DELTAS (Castro: +4 East, -3 West in CUB) so a bloc that pre-positioned can absorb or exploit them, with `SetAlignment` reserved for treaty facts (NATO accession, Warsaw Pact 1955) that set a structural floor. Wir sind das Volk! (Histogame 2014) supplies the domestic-mirror coupling in the same register: East German unrest is driven by the living-standard gap vs the West, protests are crushed at a prestige cost, and the Wall (1961) is a card that stops emigration; that is the consumer-goods gap already computed by the planned-economy substrate feeding satellite drift, with a Crackdown verb that restores control at a world-opinion price (Berlin June 1953, Hungary Nov 1956).
findings.evidence: TS rules §5.2 (opponent events), §7 (Space Race); Wir sind das Volk! rules (unrest, prosperity, Prestige, Wall card); repo: docs/design/systems/world-timeline.md (SetAlignment, OptionChosen, Independence), assets/data/scenario/1950/events/*.ron (29 SetAlignment uses), assets/data/scenario/1950/countries/independence.ron, crates/ugs-sim/src/construction.rs ProjectPayload::Prestige.

findings.title: Balance of Power (1985) is the earliest digital version of the same contest and its one durable idea is that every influence act is also an escalation probe priced by prior commitment
findings.detail: Chris Crawford's Balance of Power (Mindscape 1985; 1990 edition) runs ~60 countries with government and insurgency strengths; superpower verbs are economic aid, military aid, insurgency aid, destabilization, diplomatic pressure, treaties, and intervention. Any move the rival objects to opens a crisis where each side escalates or backs down; backing down costs prestige scaled by how much you had previously invested in that country, and prestige is the score. The lesson for coupling pillar 2 to pillar 1: the tension cost of an influence act should scale with the OTHER side's stake in the target (their influence there, their treaty status, superpower adjacency), not with the act alone. Couping a country the rival controls is a provocation; couping an empty one is news. That is TS's battleground rule generalized, and it is what turns the map's painted state into an escalation landscape the player reads before acting.
findings.evidence: Balance of Power (Crawford, 1985; 'Balance of Power: The 1990 Edition'), Crawford's design notes in 'Balance of Power: International Politics as the Ultimate Global Game' (Microsoft Press 1986); repo: docs/design/systems/escalation.md crisis ladder and resolve, docs/design/systems/war-termination.md red-line penalty (adjacency to another bloc's divisions).

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Two influence piles per country with a stability-margin control test (the TS substrate)
mechanics_recommendations.why: It is the minimum state that makes alignment a contest: three integers, a derived control, and the existing three-valued enum becomes a projection instead of the source of truth. Denial-cheaper-than-acquisition falls out of the placement cost rule and produces the non-aligned middle without a third AI.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Per-country `influence: (west: u8, east: u8)` on the world-state resource alongside the existing `alignments`/`stability` overrides; `stab = clamp(round(stability/20),1,5)`; `net = west - east`; `alignment_of` returns Western if net >= stab, Eastern if net <= -stab, else NonAligned, with treaty/satellite status (events, war-termination client states) as a structural floor that realignment cannot remove. Seed 1950 from TS's setup list adjusted to Jan 1950 (US: UK 5, France 3, Italy 2, W.Germany 3, Japan 1, S.Korea 1, Iran 1, Israel 1, Australia 4, Canada 2, Panama 1; USSR: E.Germany 3, Poland 3, Finland 1, Syria 1, Iraq 1, N.Korea 3, PRC treaty floor Feb 1950) and a historian pass on per-country stability replacing the flat 60. Read by the player as TS-style pips on an INFLUENCE map mode and a one-line verdict per country ('IRAN LEANS WEST; ONE SOVIET POINT BREAKS CONTROL'). Decision changed: where to spend this month's scarce ops.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Verb split: standing programs (aid, propaganda) as monthly +1 flows in capped slots; discrete ops (pressure/realignment, coup, election interference) as event-shaped rolls
mechanics_recommendations.why: Board games make every act discrete, but the espionage house rules forbid upkeep micro and require pull decisions. Aid and propaganda are historically continuous (Marshall Plan, PL-480, Radio Free Europe) while coups and elections are discrete gambles; separating them keeps the decision count fixed at the slot cap and lets each verb differ in speed, deniability, and tension.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Superpowers get ~6 program slots, mid-powers 2, others 0; a slot assigns one country and one kind (AID: +1 own influence/month, costs stock from the economy, +1 stability over time; PROPAGANDA: +1/month only into popular sympathy in v1.5, deniable, weaker in closed regimes). Discrete ops: PRESSURE = TS realignment roll (own d6 + adjacent controlled + lead + superpower-adjacent vs rival's), costs 1 op, visible; COUP = `d6 + network_tier - 2*stab` through `intel.rs` LaunchOperation with the outcome ladder, spends the network, tension +15 in battlegrounds / +5 elsewhere, PROVEN attribution banks a pretext; ELECTION = a pressure roll scheduled for a democracy's election date (data: Italy Jun 1953, W.Germany, France, Chile, etc.), doubled effect if clean, reversed and world-opinion cost if blown. Read as a per-op card showing frontier and ladder, never a percentage. Decision changed: which of the three prices (money, tension, deniability) to pay for a given flip.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Scoring regions with battlegrounds, Presence/Domination/Control tiers, checkpoint scoring, and an 'IF SCORED TODAY' newspaper page
mechanics_recommendations.why: Without a scoreboard 123 countries is a list. TS's tier rule concentrates play on ~30 named countries, gives victory a computable object at 1955/1960/1965/1970, and hands every AI bloc a utility gradient (COIN-bot-style ranked predicates) with no bespoke AI.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Data file `assets/data/scenario/1950/influence/regions.ron`: eight regions (Europe, Middle East, South Asia, East Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, North Africa folded into ME or Africa by historian call, Central America/Caribbean, South America) each with a battleground set and tier values seeded from TS (Europe 3/7/win-equivalent, Asia 3/7/9, ME 3/5/7, Africa 1/4/6, CA 1/3/5, SA 2/5/6) plus +1 per battleground and +1 per country adjacent to the rival superpower; Non-Aligned counts as denied. Compute on `new_month`; render as the newspaper's INFLUENCE STANDINGS page ('EUROPE: WEST DOMINATES (+7) - BATTLEGROUNDS 4/5') and the victory checkpoint banks the table. AI bloc monthly pick = argmax marginal scoring gain per op subject to tension gates and reach. Decision changed: the player sees which battleground is one point from flipping and spends there instead of spreading.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Tension gating and pricing lifted from DEFCON: bands close regions in war-start order, battleground coups pay tension, PROVEN coups are crisis pretexts
mechanics_recommendations.why: This is the coupling that makes pillar 2 live inside pillar 1 (espionage research principle 2): every covert act spends escalation headroom, and the Brink band forces the contest into the Third World the way DEFCON 2 does.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Gate table in `influence::tuning`: Calm/Wary all regions open; Crisis closes Europe to coups and pressure ops; Brink closes Europe, Asia, Middle East. Tension deltas in tenths: battleground coup +150, other coup +50, blown election op +60, doubled when the target is rival-controlled (Balance of Power's stake rule), and a successful coup against a rival-controlled battleground with PROVEN attribution registers a pretext with the crisis system. AI reads the band as tension.md already specifies. Read by the player as a line on the op card ('CLOSED AT CRISIS: EUROPE') and on the top-bar band. Decision changed: whether to spend the coup now at Wary or wait for the world to cool, and whether to run a coup at all while a Korea-scale war has tension at 60.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Non-Aligned as a field: saturation backlash above a stability cap, a post-Bandung regional decay from NAM champions, and 'denied' scoring
mechanics_recommendations.why: Answers the sketch's first open question with zero new AI actors: the passive middle emerges from arithmetic, the active pull is a monthly decay and a bust rule, and checkpoints reward denial so both blocs have reason to keep countries out of the other's column rather than only to paint their own.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Monthly: if either bloc's influence in a non-treaty country exceeds `stab * SATURATION (2)`, roll from `b"influence"` a backlash that removes 1-2 of that bloc's points and lowers stability (the CIA-vs-KGB bust; Iran 1979 in miniature). After the Bandung event (Apr 1955) countries adjacent to a NAM champion (a data flag on IND, EGY, YUG, IDN, later GHA) lose 1 foreign point per quarter unless treaty-floored; Belgrade 1961 widens the radius. Standings count 'denied' countries per region for the bloc that does not control them. Read as attributed wire lines ('SYRIA: NASSERIST PRESSURE ERODES SOVIET POSITION -1') and a NAM tint on the map. Decision changed: whether to push past the cap for control or settle for denial.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Decolonization as a contested opening: a pending-independence window, inherited metropole influence, anti-colonial discount, born-unstable states
mechanics_recommendations.why: Today a newborn's alignment is whatever independence.ron says and nobody competes. The timeline gives the dates; the contest must give the outcome. TS's 'Decolonization' and 'Colonial Rear Guards' cards are the precedent for both blocs pushing into the same newborns.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Twelve months before each scheduled `Independence` event the wire announces 'INDEPENDENCE PENDING' and the future tag becomes a legal influence target (reach granted to both blocs). At birth: the metropole's bloc inherits `min(2, metropole influence share)` points, the rival gets its pending placements at a 1-op-per-point rate regardless of control (anti-colonial discount), stability seeds at 1-2 (TS Africa values), and independence.ron's fixed `alignment` is replaced by these opening piles so the enum is derived. Read on the newspaper's reserved THE COLONIAL QUESTION page as a table of pending states with both blocs' pips. Decision changed: whether to spend scarce ops on a state that does not exist yet, and whether to court the metropole (UK/France, mid-powers with their own 0.5 op/month) to inherit rather than compete.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: The domestic mirror: satellites and allies carry the same piles, the rival's programs run there too, living-standard gap drives satellite drift, and a Crackdown verb trades world opinion for control
mechanics_recommendations.why: The sketch asks for the mirror; Wir sind das Volk! and A Distant Plain show it is the same contest with different scoring for allies. Reusing the piles means Radio Free Europe is just a propaganda slot on Poland and Hungary 1956 is a stability crash the Soviet player must answer.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Bloc members keep a treaty floor (cannot be realigned below control) but their popular sympathy (v1.5) drifts by the consumer-goods gap the planned-economy substrate already computes; when sympathy diverges from government control past a threshold an UPRISING event fires (Berlin 1953, Poznan/Budapest 1956, existing timeline hooks). Crackdown command: restore stability and control at +tension, -world opinion (a global modifier of -1 to the crackdown bloc's pressure rolls for N months, 13 Days' World Opinion battleground), and +1 rival propaganda effectiveness bloc-wide. Elections in allied democracies use the same election-op path, so France or Italy can elect a non-aligned government if sympathy is neglected. Read as the standings page's 'BLOC COHESION' line and uprising wire arcs. Decision changed: crush or concede, and whether to spend program slots at home instead of abroad.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Reach rule and superpower adjacency (the geography of the contest)
mechanics_recommendations.why: TS placement adjacency plus the +1 superpower-adjacent modifiers are what make Cuba and Finland prizes and make Soviet reach land-bound while American reach is naval. Without reach, ops teleport and the map's shape stops mattering.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Derive a country adjacency graph once from `ProvinceDef.adjacent` and a coastal flag. A bloc may place or pressure only where it has influence, an embassy (the intel embassy floor as presence), an adjacent controlled country, or naval reach (US: any coastal country; USSR: coastal reach unlocked by a 1960s navy event). Countries adjacent to a superpower give that superpower +1 on pressure rolls and cost the rival +1 stability-equivalent to coup; controlling a country adjacent to the rival superpower scores +1. Read as a REACH line on the country card ('NO REACH - REQUIRES EMBASSY OR ADJACENT PRESENCE'). Decision changed: build the stepping stones (Iraq before Iran, Ghana before the 1960 wave) rather than strike the prize directly.

pitfalls: Ops density: porting TS's per-action-round ops as a monthly budget overshoots 10x and paints the board; anchor total campaign ops per superpower well below the summed control thresholds (TS: ~170 ops vs 84 countries), roughly 1.5-2 ops/month in 1950, and let decay, backlash, and removal keep it scarce.

Flat stability: with 73 of 86 sovereigns at stability 60 every country is the same coup target; the whole difficulty surface is the stability table, so a sourced per-country pass (TS's printed values as the seed) must ship with the mechanic, not after it.

Snowball through adjacency: TS's realignment bonuses are balanced by card scarcity and DEFCON; a sim with no cards will run away regionally unless saturation backlash, NAM decay, and denial-cheaper-than-acquisition are in from v1 and the AI bloc actually contests battlegrounds rather than spreading presence.

Percentages and dice betrayal: exposing 'coup 62%' recreates the XCOM problem; expose the frontier (stability vs network tier) and the outcome ladder with period likelihood words, and make failure a content arc (a blown coup is a U-2-shaped story, not a modifier).

Double-writers on alignment: keeping 29 SetAlignment decrees and independence.ron fixed alignments alongside an influence contest produces cases where history overrules the player with no cause line; convert to influence deltas and treaty floors, keep one accessor, and require every monthly change to carry an attributed cause on the wire.

DEFCON suicide analog: any event option, AI priority, or forced response that compels a coup or pressure op while the band is Brink converts an influence action into a nuclear-ladder trigger; forbid it in the gate table and in content review.

Non-Aligned as a third AI player: QMG: Cold War shows it needs its own win condition and full agency; that is a v3 investment. Model it as a field and a scored outcome, and let regional AIs (Egypt, India) act through the same mid-power op budget instead.

Decision-count creep: 123 countries times three verbs is Vic3's whack-a-mole; fix the count at program slots plus one or two pull decisions a month surfaced by a briefing card, and make the map mode and standings page the place you look, not act.
analysts.first_hour_test: Playing the USA from 1950-01-01: in January the influence map mode already shows the world as pips and a verdict per country, and the newspaper's founding edition prints IF SCORED TODAY standings (Europe: WEST DOMINATES; Asia: CONTESTED; Middle East: PRESENCE only). The first monthly briefing card offers two pull decisions with the frontier printed: 'ITALY (STAB 2, BATTLEGROUND): WEST 2 / EAST 1 - ONE SOVIET POINT BREAKS CONTROL - AID SLOT AVAILABLE' and 'IRAN (STAB 2): WEST 1 / EAST 0 - TUDEH NETWORK L1 DETECTED - COUP FRONTIER OPEN'. The player fills one or two of six program slots (Italy aid, Iran aid) and queues nothing else; February's paper shows Italy at WEST 3 with the cause line 'MUTUAL SECURITY AID'. By March or April the Soviet AI, climbing the same scoring gradient, lands a visible move: a pressure op on Syria (stab 2, adjacent to Soviet-leaning Iraq) strips a Western point, tension ticks +5.0 and the wire prints it with a RESPOND? card offering a counter-pressure op at its printed roll modifiers. In May the standings page moves for the first time (Middle East: EAST PRESENCE) and the player feels the checkpoint clock (1955) as a number. On June 25 Korea fires unchanged, but the war's patron and client-state logic now reads an alignment that the player has been moving, and the tension jump into Crisis closes Europe to coups on the influence panel with a visible CLOSED AT CRISIS line. The pillar is proven playable if, before the war, the player has made two influence decisions, seen the map tint change with an attributed cause, seen the rival move once and been offered a response, and can name which battleground they will fight over next.

findings.title: Economic aid consolidated alignment it almost never converted it; the alignment effect landed at announcement and at withdrawal, not at delivery
findings.detail: The Marshall Plan (Economic Cooperation Act signed 3 Apr 1948; ~$13.3B through mid-1952, ~$3B/yr against federal outlays of ~$40B, so ~7-8% of the budget, real guns-vs-butter money) went to sixteen countries that were already Western-governed: France and Italy had expelled their communist ministers in May 1947, before a dollar arrived. Its political work was consolidation (OEEC 16 Apr 1948, counterpart-fund leverage, and a 5% counterpart skim that quietly financed OPC covert action, Pisani 1991) plus one conversion-by-denial: the Soviet walkout from the Paris talks (2 Jul 1947) and forced Czech/Polish withdrawal (10 Jul 1947) hardened the bloc line. Point Four (inaugural 20 Jan 1949; Act for International Development 5 Jun 1950; ~$34.5M first year) was technical assistance at 1/400th the Marshall scale and moved no alignments. The Soviet economic offensive after the Khrushchev-Bulganin Asian tour (Nov-Dec 1955) was 1/10th the US scale (bloc credits to non-communist developing countries ~$4-5B in 1954-64) yet had outsized effect because it was concentrated in four bidders (India, Egypt, Indonesia, Afghanistan took ~2/3) and delivered as legible showpieces: Bhilai steel (agreement 2 Feb 1955, ~647M rubles at 2.5% over 12 years, first blast furnace Feb 1959), the Aswan High Dam (Soviet credit 23 Oct 1958, 400M rubles ~$100M; second credit Jan 1960 ~900M rubles; construction 9 Jan 1960-1970), Afghanistan's $100M credit line (Dec 1955 visit) after Washington refused Kabul arms in 1954 in favor of Pakistan, Indonesia's $100M credit (Sept 1956). The decisive events were announcements and withdrawals: Dulles withdrew the US/UK/IBRD Aswan offer ($56M + $14M grants + $200M loan, offered Dec 1955) on 19 Jul 1956 and Nasser nationalized the Canal seven days later (26 Jul); the dam itself took ten years and Egypt was expelling Soviet advisers before it had aged two. For the sim: an aid offer is an event object with an announcement shock, a delivery clock, and a withdrawal option that is itself a crisis pretext; completion is the weakest of its three moments.
findings.evidence: Hogan, The Marshall Plan (1987); Milward, The Reconstruction of Western Europe 1945-51 (1984); Pisani, The CIA and the Marshall Plan (1991); Truman inaugural 20 Jan 1949; Act for International Development, 5 Jun 1950; US Dept of State RSB reports 'Communist Governments and Developing Nations: Aid and Trade' (1960s series); Heikal, Cutting the Lion's Tail (1986) on 19-26 Jul 1956; Engerman, The Price of Aid (2018) on Bhilai; Kalinovsky/Nunan on Afghanistan 1955.

findings.title: Covert regime change was nearly free in cash and paid in exposure; it succeeded roughly 4 in 10 times, and only where a local army and a local crisis already existed
findings.detail: Costs were trivial against any national budget: TPAJAX Iran (approved by Eisenhower 11 Jul 1953, executed 15-19 Aug 1953) had a $1M authorization and a working budget of $285,000 split CIA/SIS in the Wilber history; PBSUCCESS Guatemala (authorized Aug 1953, invasion 18 Jun 1954, Arbenz resigned 27 Jun) cost ~$2.7M; the Bay of Pigs (approved in outline 17 Mar 1960 at $4.4M, ballooned to ~$46M, 17-19 Apr 1961) was the expensive outlier and the loudest failure. Time-to-effect was 5-13 months from authorization. What determined success was never the dollar figure: Iran flipped because the Anglo-Iranian oil boycott (from 1951) had wrecked the economy and the army and Shia clergy were split; the first attempt (15-16 Aug) failed outright and the Shah fled to Baghdad before the 19 Aug crowds and Zahedi's tanks reversed it. Guatemala fell because 480 men and a fake radio (David Atlee Phillips' Voice of Liberation) convinced the officer corps the US Marines were coming; the army withdrew its support and Arbenz resigned without a battle. Failures (Syria Aug 1957 Operation Wappen, exposed when the officers Rocky Stone tried to buy reported him and Damascus expelled three US diplomats 12-13 Aug; Indonesia 1958, when pilot Allen Pope was shot down over Ambon 18 May carrying documents; Cuba 1961) were all against nationalist governments with a loyal army, and each moved alignment AWAY from the intervening side: Syria joined the UAR (1 Feb 1958), Sukarno bought ~$1B of Soviet arms 1958-65, Castro proclaimed the revolution socialist on 16 Apr 1961, the day before the landing. O'Rourke's dataset counts 64 US covert regime-change attempts 1947-89 with 39% installing the preferred faction, and finds even successes rarely improved relations. The sim needs covert flips gated on two visible local factors (army lean, stability/crisis) rather than cash, and needs the failure branch to move alignment the wrong way.
findings.evidence: Wilber, CIA Clandestine Service History 'Overthrow of Premier Mossadeq of Iran' (Mar 1954, declassified 2000, Appendix B budget); Cullather, Secret History: The CIA's Classified Account of Its Operations in Guatemala (1999); Pfeiffer, Official History of the Bay of Pigs Operation (declassified 2011); Jones, The Bay of Pigs (2008); Little, 'Cold War and Covert Action: The United States and Syria, 1945-1958', Middle East Journal (1990); Kahin & Kahin, Subversion as Foreign Policy (1995); O'Rourke, Covert Regime Change: America's Secret Cold War (Cornell 2018).

findings.title: Election interference bought about three points, worked best in the open and through standing local organizations, and the Italian template ran for twenty years
findings.detail: The 18 Apr 1948 Italian election is the founding case: NSC 4-A (Dec 1947) authorized covert action; CIA spent on the order of $1M (some accounts $10M) via bag-money to the DC and centrist parties; but the visible half mattered more: the Tripartite Declaration on Trieste (20 Mar 1948), Marshall 'Friendship Train' grain arriving in port with press, Truman's threat to cut aid to a communist Italy, Cardinal Spellman, Luigi Gedda's Civic Committees mobilizing the parishes, and ~10 million letters from Italian-Americans. Result: DC 48.5% vs Popular Front 31%. The lesson became policy: NSC 10/2 (18 Jun 1948) created OPC; the Pike Committee later put CIA subsidies to Italian parties at ~$65-75M for 1948-68 (a further ~$10M in 1972). Chile 1964 is the best per-voter calibration: Church Committee found ~$2.6M direct (perhaps $3-4M all in) to elect Frei in an electorate of ~2.5M, i.e. roughly a dollar a vote, comparable to US campaign spending per voter. Japan's LDP received CIA money through the 1950s-60s (NYT 9 Oct 1994). Moscow ran the mirror image through the International Department's 'International Fund for Assistance to Left Workers' Organizations' (est. 1950), several million dollars a year to the PCI alone, plus the Cominform's press. Levin's dataset of 117 partisan electoral interventions 1946-2000 (81 US, 36 USSR) measures an average +3 percentage points for the favored side, with overt help outperforming covert. Elections were also where allies drifted: Iceland's Althing voted to expel the US base (Mar 1956) and reversed after Hungary; Ceylon's Bandaranaike (Apr 1956) closed British bases; Japan's Anpo crisis (Jun 1960) cancelled Eisenhower's visit. Three points decides close races and nothing else, so the mechanic is a marginal push on a scheduled window, not a flip verb.
findings.evidence: Miller, 'Taking Off the Gloves: The United States and the Italian Elections of 1948', Diplomatic History 7 (1983); NSC 4-A (Dec 1947), NSC 10/2 (18 Jun 1948, FRUS 1945-50 Emergence of the Intelligence Establishment); Pike Committee report as leaked to the Village Voice, Feb 1976; Church Committee, Covert Action in Chile 1963-1973 (Dec 1975); Levin, Meddling in the Ballot Box (OUP 2020); Riva, Oro da Mosca (1999); Andrew & Mitrokhin, The Sword and the Shield (1999) ch. on party funding; Weiner NYT 9 Oct 1994 on LDP.

findings.title: Broadcasting, culture, students and 'peace' campaigns changed beliefs slowly and never flipped a government, but they set the world-opinion price of every crackdown and produced their own blowback
findings.detail: VOA (1942) and CIA-funded RFE (first broadcast to Czechoslovakia 4 Jul 1950, Munich from 1 May 1951) and Radio Liberation (1 Mar 1953) cost on the order of $20-35M/yr combined by the late 1950s, more than 85% covertly funded behind the Crusade for Freedom; USIA (1 Aug 1953) ran ~$80-110M/yr. Soviet jamming from 1948 onward is estimated to have cost Moscow more than the Western broadcasts themselves. Balloon leaflets 1951-56 delivered ~300M pieces. Effect: sustained opposition and denied the regimes an information monopoly (RFE surveys found roughly half of Polish adults listening by the late 1950s), but the one time listeners acted on it, Hungary Oct 23-Nov 4 1956, RFE's Hungarian service was found by internal review to have implied Western help that never came; ~2,500 Hungarians died and ~200,000 fled, and 'Radio Free Europe encouraged them' became a permanent Soviet talking point. The cultural front had the same shape: Congress for Cultural Freedom (founded West Berlin 26 Jun 1950, CIA money via the Farfield Foundation, ~$800K-900K/yr, Encounter from 1953) versus the Cominform (22-27 Sept 1947 to 17 Apr 1956), the World Peace Council's Stockholm Appeal (Mar 1950, claimed 273M signatures by Nov 1950), and the World Youth Festivals (Berlin 1951, Moscow 28 Jul-11 Aug 1957 with 34,000 delegates from 131 countries; Vienna 1959 countered by a CIA-funded student front). The exposure of CCF funding (Ramparts/NYT, spring 1967) retroactively discredited fifteen years of work. Patrice Lumumba Peoples' Friendship University (founded 5 Feb 1960, renamed 22 Feb 1961 after his death; ~3-4,000 students by the mid-60s) generated affinities on a 10-year fuse and also blowback: the Dec 1963 death of Ghanaian student Edmund Assare-Addo produced the first Red Square protest and soured African opinion. Hungary and Suez in the same fortnight (Nov 1956) is the calibration for the 'mirror': the PCI lost a swathe of intellectuals and members, and Britain and France lost the Arab street. Propaganda in the sim should therefore be a slow modifier on faction lean and a multiplier on the world-opinion cost the OTHER side pays for coercion, never an alignment mover in itself.
findings.evidence: Puddington, Broadcasting Freedom: The Cold War Triumph of RFE and RL (2000); Cummings, Cold War Radio (2009); Johnson, Radio Free Europe and Radio Liberty: The CIA Years and Beyond (2010) on the 1956 review; Saunders, Who Paid the Piper? The CIA and the Cultural Cold War (1999); Coleman, The Liberal Conspiracy (1989); Wernicke on the WPC, 'The Communist-led World Peace Council and the Western Peace Movements', Peace & Change (1998); Koivunen on the 1957 Moscow festival; Matusevich, 'Journeys of Hope: African Diaspora and the Soviet Society', African Diaspora (2008); Hungary casualty figures from the UN Special Committee report (1957).

findings.title: The Non-Aligned were an active third attractor who auctioned alignment; the superpowers' best 'wins' among them were denials, and aid bought access, never loyalty
findings.detail: Every leader who mattered outside the blocs ran the same play: take the first bloc's offer, show it to the second, extract more, and jail the first bloc's local party. Nasser accepted the Czech arms deal (announced 27 Sept 1955, ~$80M nominal, ~$250M in later accounting: MiG-15s, Il-28s, ~230 tanks, paid in cotton), used it to draw the Dec 1955 Western Aswan offer, recognized Peking (16 May 1956) and lost the offer, took Soviet dam credits (1958, 1960), crushed the Egyptian communists (1959) to Khrushchev's public fury, took ~$1B of US PL-480 food 1959-65 under Kennedy, and his successor expelled ~15,000 Soviet advisers on 18 Jul 1972 after seventeen years and several billion dollars of Soviet arms. Tito, expelled from the Cominform 28 Jun 1948, was 'kept afloat' by ~$1.5-2.5B of US economic and military aid 1949-60 (Emergency Relief Act Nov 1950, MDAP agreement 14 Nov 1951) and gave the West exactly a non-aligned Yugoslavia: no NATO, a Balkan Pact with Greece and Turkey (28 Feb 1953 / Bled 9 Aug 1954), the Belgrade Declaration with Khrushchev (2 Jun 1955), the Brioni meeting with Nehru and Nasser (18-19 Jul 1956), and the founding Non-Aligned conference (Belgrade 1-6 Sept 1961, 25 states) after Bandung (18-24 Apr 1955, 29 states). Sekou Toure's Guinea voted 'non' on 28 Sept 1958, was stripped by France within weeks, was ignored by Eisenhower (no ambassador until 1959), took a Soviet 140M-ruble (~$35M) credit in Aug 1959, then expelled Soviet ambassador Solod in Dec 1961 over the 'teachers' plot', visited Kennedy (Oct 1962) and refused Soviet aircraft refueling at Conakry during the missile crisis. Sukarno took the largest Soviet arms package outside the Warsaw Pact and the army that received it slaughtered the PKI in 1965-66 and flipped the country West. Nkrumah's Ghana (independent 6 Mar 1957) took Volta River money from Kaiser/US/UK/IBRD (approved by Kennedy Dec 1961) and Soviet credits (160M rubles, 1960) simultaneously until the 24 Feb 1966 coup. Finland (YYA treaty 6 Apr 1948, declined Marshall aid Jul 1947, 'night frost' Dec 1958, 'note crisis' 30 Oct 1961, Porkkala returned Jan 1956) and Austria (State Treaty 15 May 1955, neutrality law 26 Oct 1955, after ~$1B of Marshall aid) show the other face: neutrality as a negotiated superpower settlement with a standing veto on the neutral's cabinet politics. Of the eight largest Soviet aid recipients of 1955-65 (Egypt, India, Indonesia, Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, Ghana, Guinea), by 1975 only Afghanistan, India, Syria and Iraq were still close and none was a satellite. For the sim: Non-Aligned must be a state with its own prestige currency (conference hosting, mediation, votes) that lets a country extract bids from both blocs, and the correct scoring for a superpower is often 'denied to the rival', not 'gained'.
findings.evidence: Lees, Keeping Tito Afloat: The United States, Yugoslavia, and the Cold War (1997); Heikal, Sphinx and Commissar (1978); Laron, Origins of the Suez Crisis (2013) on the Czech deal; Schayegh/Westad, The Global Cold War (2005); Mazov, A Distant Front in the Cold War: The USSR in West Africa and the Congo 1956-1964 (2010) on Guinea; Muehlenbeck, Betting on the Africans: JFK's Courting of African Nationalist Leaders (2012); Kalinovsky & Radchenko on Soviet Third World aid; Jakobson, Finnish Neutrality (1968); Bischof, Austria in the First Cold War (1999); Sadat expulsion 18 Jul 1972 (Heikal, The Road to Ramadan, 1975).

findings.title: Military aid and officer training were the durable alignment lock, and supporting an unstable client produced the most violent flips in the whole era
findings.detail: The Truman Doctrine's $400M to Greece and Turkey (22 May 1947), MDAP ($1.3B, 6 Oct 1949) and the Mutual Security Act (10 Oct 1951, ~$7.5B first year) created the pattern the Soviets copied after 1955: hardware brings advisers, advisers bring training, training brings a generation of officers whose careers and spare parts depend on the patron. The coups that stuck (Iran 1953, Guatemala 1954, Congo's Mobutu 14 Sept 1960 after Devlin's station was authorized an initial ~$100,000 for anti-Lumumba politicians, Brazil 31 Mar 1964 with a carrier group offshore and ~$5M of 1962 election money, Indonesia Oct 1965) were all carried by armies already inside the patron's training and supply web. The same web also produced the era's worst blowback: Iraq took Baghdad Pact membership (1955) into the 14 Jul 1958 revolution and left the pact 24 Mar 1959; Batista's US-armed Cuba became Castro's; Ethiopia's Kagnew base deal (1953) became the Derg (1974); Iran 1953 became Iran 1979; Somalia, Sudan and Egypt did the same to Moscow. The rule visible in the record: a patron identified with a regime of low stability inherits the successor's hostility in proportion to how visible the patronage was. For the sim: the army is a faction with its own patron and equipment lineage; a coup verb requires the army's lean; a client with low stability is a liability whose successor spawns already leaning against you; ClientState and Neutralization clauses from war-termination should write into this same faction ledger.
